title: Small allocation amplification and CUDA retry patterns — investigation notes
content:
Summary:
This note captures a set of experiments and operational observations about two related phenomena we keep seeing in production: 1) small-allocation amplification (lots of tiny allocations leading to unexpectedly large resident memory and fragmentation) and 2) transient cudaMalloc/cudaMallocAsync retry behavior that manifests as mid-run OOM spikes. The goal is to record measurements, root-cause hypotheses, quick mitigations we applied, and next experiments.

Environment snapshot (runs referenced below):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (prod cluster), occasional tests on A10G (48GB).
- Driver / CUDA: NVIDIA driver 546.x, CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.x
- Serving runtime: rwinfer/serving-runtime@main commit 2025-02-05 (includes allocator v2 experimental flags)
- Allocator modes exercised: system cudaMalloc/cudaFree, cudamallocasync (CMSA), internal slab pool (our arena allocator), pinned host staging buffers

Incident pattern observed:
- Production traces show requests that are nominal (short context, few tokens) suddenly triggering OOMs on otherwise healthy nodes.
- NVML output during incidents shows GPU memory used jumps ~2–6 GB briefly then returns to baseline after a few seconds.
- Stack traces (when available) point to allocation paths inside workspace growth code + kv-cache mispredictions (we often reallocate workspace to append new tokens).
- Telemetry: allocation churn rate spikes (allocs/sec) and a long tail in allocation latency distribution — many allocations complete in <1ms but a small fraction take 50–200ms and coincide with OOMs.

Key observations and measurements:
1) Allocation size amplification:
- Workload: many internal allocations ranged 256–16k bytes (small objects). Our allocator rounds up to 64k granularity for arenas in the current slab policy leading to an amplification factor of ~8–256x depending on distribution.
- Measurement: instrumented allocator to log requested_size and backing_size; median requested small allocation = 2.1kB, median backing size = 64kB when using arena fallback. Measured effective resident usage for the same logical payload rose by ~4x compared to a compacting allocation strategy.

2) cudaMallocAsync vs cudaMalloc behavior:
- With cudaMallocAsync enabled, we saw reduced average latency for short-lived buffers but delayed physical decommit: freed async blocks are returned to the CUDA async pool and not immediately released to OS, causing transient high-water marks of resident memory when new allocations occur concurrently.
- In a stress test with 200 concurrent short requests, cudamallocasync produced stable throughput but occasional 2–4 second windows where available memory dipped below requested and the driver began retrying allocations.
- Retry traces: we observed loops where cudaMallocAsync returns error codes after internal retries and then succeeds later (observed via exponential backoff in our wrapper). Those transient fails often coincide with other processes on the GPU (e.g., background profiler job) freeing memory a few hundred ms later.

3) Fragmentation metrics and contiguous free space:
- We implemented a lightweight probe that attempts to cudaMalloc contiguous blocks decreasing by power-of-two to estimate largest_contiguous_free. During incidents the largest_contiguous_free was often < 10% of total_free, indicative of external fragmentation.
- Calculated fragmentation metric used in telemetry: frag_ratio = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free / total_free). Median frag_ratio during normal ops ~0.18; during incidents >0.65.

4) Allocation latency and stall correlation:
- NVTX-marked traces show long allocation latencies align with request tail latency spikes. When allocation retries occur, request workers block and the request times out or crashes.

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked):
A) Small-allocation rounding + slab reservation policy: many 1–8k allocations map to dedicated 64k slabs that persist per-stream. Over time these partially-used slabs fragment GPU address space.
B) cudamallocasync pooled freelist semantics + delayed physical reclaim: freed memory returns to the CUDA async pool instead of being returned to OS, so a burst of transient allocations from other streams can exhaust the pool and cause driver-side retries.
C) Mixed allocation lifetimes across contexts: long-lived KV cache entries intermixed with ephemeral workspaces cause fragmentation in shared arenas.
D) External noise: other tenants or background jobs allocate, free, or pin host pages (UC/managed memory) causing momentary pressure and triggering retries.

Experiments performed (summary):
1) Microbenchmark: small-alloc churn
- Setup: 128 worker threads each allocating 2–8k buffers and freeing them after 10–200ms. Compared allocator modes.
- Result: system cudaMalloc had lower peak resident but higher allocation latency. cudamallocasync had lowest mean latency but highest peak resident memory due to pooled freelists. Custom slab with per-size freelists reduced resident peak by ~35% at cost of ~12% higher average allocation latency.

2) Deliberate decommit test
- Force calling cudaMemRelease (CUDA 12.2) after free in a branch of the runtime vs leaving freed mem in pool. Observed that explicit release reduced peak resident usage but increased average allocation latency and introduced occasional blocking on release.

3) Coalescing and hole reuse experiments
- Modified arena to attempt coalescing adjacent free blocks before returning to CUDA. This reduced frag_ratio in synthetic patterns by ~20% and increased largest_contiguous_free by ~1.7x. Works well for long-lived mixed allocations but adds CPU overhead.

4) Retry watchdog and fast-fail policy
- Added a max-retry window (200ms) for allocation attempts; if exceeded we return an ENOMEM to caller immediately and trigger a low-priority background defrag job. This reduces request tail latency but increases failed requests under high contention.

Applied mitigations in production (short-term):
- Enable per-stream small-object arenas with tighter slab sizing: change slab granularity from 64k -> 16k for sizes <= 16k. This reduced small-allocation amplification in canary pool by ~2.3x.
- Add allocation retry watchdog to prevent indefinite blocking; also surfaced a clearer error code to the API so callers can retry at app-level with backoff.
- Backpressure at router: limit concurrent short-lived requests per-GPU to cap alloc churn; this is conservative but prevented a handful of P1s.

Tradeoffs observed:
- Smaller slab granularity reduces amplification but increases metadata overhead and slightly higher fragmentation due to more free lists.
- Immediate cudaMemRelease reduces peaks but is expensive and increases latency variance.
- Aggressive coalescing reduces fragmentation but requires more CPU time and complexity in lock management.

Repro steps for engineering to validate locally:
1) Checkout commit: rwinfer/serving-runtime@main (2025-02-05) and enable flags: --alloc-mode=experimental-per-stream --slab-granularity=16k --cudamallocasync=on/ off to compare
2) Run microbench: scripts/bench/small_alloc_churn.py --workers 128 --size-dist small --duration 600 --report-interval 10
3) Collect telemetry: nvprof / nsight metrics + allocator logs (enable ALLOC_TRACE=1). Also run probe_largest_free.sh to sample contiguous free bytes every 5s (script in tools/).

Recommended medium-term fixes (engineer-facing):
- Implement hybrid pool: preallocate size-class pools for common small sizes (512B, 2KB, 8KB) with tight packing and fast freelists; keep cudamallocasync for bigger chunks and GPU-resident caches.
- Add a background defragmenter that runs during low-load windows and attempts coalescing + cudaMemRelease for large returned shards.
- Improve telemetry: expose frag_ratio and largest_contiguous_free to Console dashboards, add alerts when frag_ratio > 0.5 for >30s.
- Allocation admission control: make the request router aware of current frag_ratio/available_contiguous and reject or redirect to a lower-memory model variant when contiguity is insufficient.

Open questions and next experiments:
- Does decreasing slab granularity to 8k provide materially better results for typical production traces? CPU overhead vs memory tradeoff needs measurement.
- Can we leverage GPU virtualization features (MIG-like isolation on supported hardware) to fence noisy tenants that cause transient retries?
- Evaluate impact of turning off cudamallocasync cluster-wide for a short time window to see ops impact — earlier tests show reduced throughput but fewer OOMs; need controlled canary.
- Explore transparent spill-to-host for ephemeral workspace allocations (trade network/PCIe cost vs OOM prevention).

Appendix: quick logs and snippets
- Example allocator log (trimmed):

  [2025-02-18T15:12:03.189Z] free id=45123 delayed_to_pool age_ms=47
  [2025-02-18T15:12:03.220Z] alloc_request id=45124 size=8192 backing=65536 mode=arena stream=0x7f2
  [2025-02-18T15:12:03.299Z] cudaMallocAsync failed after retries id=45125 requested=1048576 err=CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY retry_ms=120
  [2025-02-18T15:12:03.428Z] cudaMallocAsync succeeded id=45125 requested=1048576 backing=1048576

- Probe script output sample (largest contiguous free)
  t=0s total_free=7.8GB largest_free=4.2GB frag_ratio=0.46
  t=12s total_free=5.6GB largest_free=0.4GB frag_ratio=0.93  <-- incident window

Notes for on-call: if you see a sustained frag_ratio > 0.7 and repeated cudaMallocAsync retry logs, take node out of rotation and trigger the defrag job (tools/defrag/run_defrag.sh) before re-adding. If re-add fails repeatedly, escalate to eng-serving-runtime and include NVML snapshot and allocator logs.

Authors and ack: Liam Patel (owner), help from Maya Chen (benchmarks), Diego Alvarez (allocator changes), Ruth Kim (prod rollout and monitoring).

End of note.
